headline: Retail prices of all major fuels increased by Tk 20 per litre
summary: The government's decision comes amid high food prices and inflationary pressure, sparking protests from political parties and concerns over rising production costs.
details: The government has increased the retail prices of all major fuels by Tk 20 per litre, effective from midnight on September 20. This decision was driven by the international energy situation and comes as citizens already face inflationary pressure from high food prices.

Bangladesh is facing a severe energy shock due to rising crude and refined product prices, disrupted shipping routes, and a weakening taka. Since the country relies heavily on imported petroleum, domestic costs are affected by exchange rates, freight insurance, and taxes.

The government attributed the increase to the Middle East conflict, which reportedly more than doubled international petroleum prices and raised freight costs. Additionally, the Bangladesh Petroleum Corporation (BPC) reportedly suffered losses of Tk 22,875.66 crore between March and August.

Rising oil prices are expected to ripple across the economy, increasing the cost of producing and transporting food, fertiliser, and raw materials. This is likely to push up transport fares for buses, trucks, and ride-sharing vehicles.

Low-income families are expected to feel the most impact, as the cost of essential goods rises. This may lead many to cut back on nutritious food, healthcare, or children's education to manage the cost of living.

The agriculture sector will face pressure in irrigation, land preparation, and fishing. Small farmers, who cannot easily raise their prices, will see reduced profits while consumers pay more due to higher transport and marketing costs.

Industries will face higher logistics and backup costs, particularly those relying on diesel generators due to unreliable electricity and gas supplies. Export industries may see reduced profits and competitiveness due to pre-negotiated prices.

Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the most vulnerable, as they have lower working capital and weaker bargaining power. For many, it could be difficult to maintain production or current working hours.

headline_marked: CUET students [[enforce complete shutdown]] over VC removal
headline: CUET students enforce complete shutdown over VC removal
summary: Students and teachers at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology have halted all academic activities demanding the reinstatement of Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem.
details: Students at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) have locked the main campus gate and launched a 'complete shutdown' to protest the removal of the Vice-Chancellor.
The protest has halted all classes, examinations, and academic activities across all departments since Tuesday morning.
Students are demanding the immediate reinstatement of Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem, who was removed from the post after only 56 days in office.
The protesters stated they will not accept the appointment of a new Vice-Chancellor and will continue their movement until Professor Sayem is restored to his position.
The CUET Teachers' Association also joined the protest, holding a human chain in front of the VC building to support the students' demands.
The university's Registrar, Professor Humayun Kabir, expressed his support for the demand to reinstate the former Vice-Chancellor.
The unrest began with a protest march on Monday night, during which students locked the VC building before escalating to the full campus shutdown on Tuesday.
caption:
Campus locked, classes halted. CUET students launch a 'complete shutdown' to demand the return of their VC.

Students at Chittagong University of Engineering and Technology (CUET) have locked the main campus gate and launched a 'complete shutdown' to protest the removal of the Vice-Chancellor.

The protest has halted all classes, examinations, and academic activities across all departments since Tuesday morning.

Students are demanding the immediate reinstatement of Professor Abu Sadat Muhammad Sayem, who was removed from the post after only 56 days in office.

The protesters stated they will not accept the appointment of a new Vice-Chancellor and will continue their movement until Professor Sayem is restored to his position.

The CUET Teachers' Association also joined the protest, holding a human chain in front of the VC building to support the students' demands.

The university's Registrar, Professor Humayun Kabir, expressed his support for the demand to reinstate the former Vice-Chancellor.

The unrest began with a protest march on Monday night, during which students locked the VC building before escalating to the full campus shutdown on Tuesday.
